entries.rule: Address Mexican military personnel using their rank followed by their last name, similar to how it's done in US military culture.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with Mexican Air Force officers
examples.say: Capitán García, ¿cómo está usted?
examples.why: The rank is omitted, which can be seen as disrespectful.

examples.situation: Briefing with Mexican military personnel
examples.say: Teniente Coronel Martínez, por favor, proceda con su informe.
examples.dontSay: Oye, Martínez, sigue con tu informe.
examples.why: The rank is omitted, and the informal 'oye' and 'tu' are inappropriate in a formal briefing.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: When addressing Mexican military personnel, use the formal 'usted' instead of the informal 'tú' to show respect for their rank and position.

examples.situation: Office visit with a Mexican Air Force colonel
examples.say: ¿Cómo está usted, Coronel Rodríguez?
examples.why: The informal 'tú' form '¿Qué tal?' is inappropriate for addressing a superior officer.

examples.situation: Gate meeting with Mexican military personnel
examples.say: Buenos días, Capitán López. ¿Cómo está usted?
examples.dontSay: Buenos días, Capitán López. ¿Qué tal tú?
examples.why: The informal 'tú' form '¿Qué tal tú?' is inappropriate for addressing a superior officer.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: When speaking with local civilians in Mexico, use the informal 'tú' and their first name unless they are much older or in a position of authority, in which case use 'usted' and their last name.

examples.situation: Meal with counterparts and their families
examples.say: ¿Qué tal, Juan? ¿Cómo estás?
examples.why: The formal 'usted' and last name are inappropriate for addressing someone who is not much older or in a position of authority.

examples.situation: Meeting with a local community leader
examples.say: Buenos días, Señor González. ¿Cómo está usted?
examples.why: The informal 'tú' form '¿Qué tal?' is inappropriate for addressing someone who is much older or in a position of authority.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Use polite and indirect expressions when refusing requests or offers to maintain harmony.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting, declined offer to attend a social event
examples.say: Agradezco la invitación, pero tengo otros compromisos.
examples.dontSay: No quiero ir a tu evento.
examples.why: The direct refusal is rude and may cause offense.

examples.situation: Gate, refused entry to a restricted area
examples.say: Lo siento, pero no está autorizado para entrar en esta área.
examples.why: The direct refusal lacks politeness and may escalate tension.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Use conditional verb forms to soften refusals and make them more acceptable.

examples.situation: Briefing, declined to provide specific information
examples.say: Podría no ser la persona adecuada para responder esa pregunta.
examples.why: The direct refusal may make you appear unhelpful.

examples.situation: Office visit, refused a request for a favor
examples.say: Me gustaría ayudarte, pero no estoy seguro de poder hacerlo.
examples.why: The direct refusal may seem harsh and uncooperative.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Provide an alternative or reason when refusing to make the refusal more palatable.

examples.situation: Meal with counterparts, refused a dish offered
examples.say: No, gracias. Estoy lleno, pero todo se ve delicioso.
examples.why: The direct refusal is impolite and may offend the host.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting, refused to agree with a suggestion
examples.say: Entiendo tu punto, pero quizá haya otra manera de abordar esto.
examples.why: The direct refusal may disrupt the collaborative atmosphere.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Use formal language and maintain respect when apologizing to Mexican Air Force members, as they value professionalism and hierarchy.

examples.situation: During a liaison meeting, you accidentally misrepresent a fact.
examples.say: Lamento mucho la confusión que causé. Por favor, permítanme corregirlo.
examples.dontSay: Lo siento, fue un error tonto.
examples.why: The informal apology can come across as disrespectful in a formal military setting.

examples.situation: At a briefing, you interrupt a Mexican Air Force officer.
examples.say: Mis disculpas por interrumpir, señor. No fue mi intención.
examples.why: Using 'señor' shows respect for the officer's rank and position.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Express gratitude sincerely and specifically when thanking Mexican Air Force members, as they appreciate acknowledgment of their efforts.

examples.situation: After a successful joint exercise, you want to thank your Mexican counterparts.
examples.say: Aprecio mucho su dedicación y esfuerzo durante este ejercicio. Gracias por su excelente trabajo.
examples.why: A general 'thanks for everything' lacks specificity and may seem insincere.

examples.situation: A Mexican Air Force officer helps you with a translation.
examples.say: Muchas gracias por su ayuda con la traducción. Realmente lo aprecio.
examples.why: Using informal language and idioms can undermine the sincerity of your thanks.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: When interacting with local civilians, use polite and respectful language when apologizing and thanking, as Mexicans value courtesy and good manners.

examples.situation: You accidentally bump into a civilian while walking through a market.
examples.say: Disculpe, por favor. No fue mi intención tropezar con usted.
examples.dontSay: Perdón, no miré por dónde iba.
examples.why: A more formal apology shows respect and consideration for the other person.

examples.situation: A local civilian helps you find your way to a specific location.
examples.say: Le agradezco mucho su ayuda. Fue muy amable de su parte.
examples.why: Using informal terms like 'tío' can be disrespectful to strangers.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Discuss family in a positive and general way; avoid sensitive topics like marital issues or family conflicts.

examples.situation: Meal with counterparts
examples.say: Mi familia es muy unida y nos gusta pasar tiempo juntos.
examples.dontSay: Mi esposa y yo estamos pasando por un momento difícil.
examples.why: Mexicans value family unity, and discussing personal conflicts can make others uncomfortable.

examples.situation: Office visit
examples.say: Tengo dos hijos y les encanta jugar fútbol.
examples.dontSay: Mi hijo mayor tiene problemas en la escuela.
examples.why: Sharing positive aspects of family life is appreciated, while negative topics can be seen as inappropriate.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Compliment Mexican culture and traditions; avoid comparisons that might imply superiority.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting
examples.say: La historia y las tradiciones de México son fascinantes.
examples.dontSay: En Estados Unidos hacemos las cosas de manera diferente.
examples.why: Mexicans take pride in their culture, and comparisons can be perceived as disrespectful.

examples.situation: Briefing
examples.say: Me encanta la arquitectura y la comida tradicional mexicana.
examples.dontSay: Nuestras ciudades son más modernas que las de México.
examples.why: Expressing genuine appreciation for Mexican culture is well-received, while boasting about one's own culture is not.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Avoid discussing sensitive political topics like drug trafficking or immigration; stick to neutral or positive subjects.

examples.situation: Gate
examples.say: ¿Qué deportes son populares en esta región?
examples.dontSay: He oído que hay mucho problema con el narcotráfico aquí.
examples.why: Bringing up sensitive political issues can create tension and discomfort.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting
examples.say: He escuchado que la música y el arte son muy importantes en México.
examples.dontSay: ¿Por qué tanta gente de México quiere emigrar a Estados Unidos?
examples.why: Focusing on positive aspects of Mexican culture is safer and more appreciated than discussing controversial topics.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Express disagreement politely and indirectly, focusing on the issue rather than the person.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with Mexican Air Force counterparts.
examples.say: Entiendo tu punto, pero perhaps we could consider another approach.
examples.dontSay: Tu idea no va a funcionar.
examples.why: The second phrase is too direct and can be seen as confrontational.

examples.situation: Briefing with local civilians in Mexico.
examples.say: Me pregunto si hay otra manera de ver esto.
examples.why: The second phrase is disrespectful and can damage relationships.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Use

examples.situation: Office visit with Mexican Air Force personnel.
examples.say: Tengo una preocupación sobre este punto. ¿Podríamos discutirlo más?
examples.why: The second phrase is too blunt and can be seen as dismissive.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Avoid interrupting and allow others to finish speaking before expressing disagreement.

examples.situation: Gate meeting with Mexican Air Force and local civilians.
examples.say: Gracias por compartir tu opinión. Me gustaría ofrecer otra perspectiva.
examples.why: The second phrase is disrespectful and can escalate tensions.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Accept all offers of food or drink to show respect and avoid causing offense.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with Mexican Air Force officers who offer coffee.
examples.say: Sí, por favor. Eso sería muy amable.
examples.why: Refusing outright can be seen as rude or dismissive.

examples.situation: Office visit where a colleague offers you a snack.
examples.say: Ahorita, gracias.
examples.dontSay: No, no quiero comer nada ahora.
examples.why: Using 'ahorita' politely defers without outright refusal.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Offer to help with cleanup after a meal to demonstrate goodwill and respect for the host.

examples.situation: Meal with Mexican Air Force counterparts at their base.
examples.say: ¿Puedo ayudar a limpiar?
examples.dontSay: Me voy ahora. Fue una buena comida.
examples.why: Leaving without offering help can be perceived as impolite.

examples.situation: Dining with local civilians at a restaurant.
examples.say: Déjenme ayudar con los platos.
examples.dontSay: Voy a irme. Fue una cena deliciosa.
examples.why: Offering to help shows appreciation and respect.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Linger after meals to engage in conversation, as this is a common and appreciated practice.

examples.situation: Lunch with Mexican Air Force officers.
examples.say: ¿Qué tal si seguimos hablando un poco más?
examples.dontSay: Tengo que irme ahora. Fue una comida rápida.
examples.why: Leaving immediately can be seen as abrupt and impolite.

examples.situation: Dinner with local civilians at their home.
examples.say: Me encanta la conversación. Sigamos hablando.
examples.dontSay: Estoy cansado. Me voy a la cama.
examples.why: Staying to chat shows you value their company.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Use expressive gestures to show engagement, but avoid overly exaggerated movements that might seem disrespectful.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with Mexican Air Force officers
examples.say: ¡Qué interesante!
examples.why: ¡Increíble! can come across as overly enthusiastic and insincere in formal settings.

examples.situation: Briefing with local civilians
examples.say: Estoy de acuerdo.
examples.why: ¡Totalmente de acuerdo! might seem too emphatic and could undermine the seriousness of the discussion.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Maintain appropriate eye contact to show attentiveness, but avoid staring as it can be perceived as aggressive.

examples.situation: Office visit with a Mexican Air Force commander
examples.say: Entiendo su punto.
examples.why: Repetitive affirmations with sustained eye contact can be seen as confrontational.

examples.situation: Gate meeting with Mexican Air Force personnel
examples.say: Por favor, explique nuevamente.
examples.why: Saying 'No entiendo' without maintaining eye contact can be perceived as dismissive or disinterested.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

entries.rule: Avoid long silences in conversations, as they are often perceived as uncomfortable; fill gaps with polite comments or questions.

examples.situation: Meal with Mexican Air Force counterparts
examples.say: ¿Cómo está su familia?
examples.why: Silence during a meal can be seen as rude or disinterested in Mexican culture.

examples.situation: Liaison meeting with Mexican Air Force officers
examples.say: Interesante perspectiva.
examples.why: Allowing silence to linger can make the other party feel uncomfortable or unheard.
